strengths: Interesting and intuitive motivation: Unlike existing training-free DiT acceleration techniques that apply spatially uniform pruning/caching or rely solely on low-level feature similarity, AccelAes leverages the spatial non-uniformity induced by aesthetic descriptors in prompts to guide compute allocation.

Comprehensive and rigorous experimental protocol: Evaluated on 10,000 Pick-a-Pic prompts with multiple seeds (30,000 images per setting) across three modern DiT architectures (Lumina-Next-T2I, SD3-Medium, FLUX.1-dev) against several competitive baselines (e.g., TeaCache, TaylorSeer, Delta-DiT, RAS, SDiT).

Solid empirical trade-off: Demonstrates tangible end-to-end runtime speedups (up to 2.11x on Lumina-Next-T2I on modern hardware) while preserving or improving automated preference and alignment metrics (ImageReward, HPSv2, CLIP score).

Detailed ablation and sensitivity analysis: The paper includes extensive ablations dissecting the contributions of AesMask, spatial attention/FFN sparsification, StepCache, anchor weighting strategies, mask step timing, and token skip ratios.
weaknesses: Limited architectural generality for the spatial components: As noted in the appendix, the complete AesMask + SkipSparse framework is only fully functional on Lumina-Next. On SD3-Medium, spatial CFG had to be disabled due to instability in MMDiT joint text-image blocks, and on FLUX.1-dev, spatial SkipSparse could not be applied at all (relying almost exclusively on temporal StepCache). This weakens the claim of a universally applicable spatio-temporal framework across modern DiTs.

Confounding source of quality improvement: AccelAes reports higher ImageReward and Aesthetic scores than the dense baseline. However, part of this gain appears to stem from spatial CFG modulation (applying higher guidance to foreground/aesthetic regions) rather than the acceleration itself. An ablation clarifying how much quality gain comes from spatial CFG versus sparse compute would help disentangle guidance enhancement from inference acceleration.

Heuristic anchor dictionary and prompt dependency: AesMask depends on a predefined, hardcoded list of 34 English anchor words. Analysis shows that anchors are only triggered in ~45-65% of prompts, requiring an unweighted fallback on the rest. The method's effectiveness on prompts with implicit aesthetic cues or domain-specific language remains somewhat constrained.

Absence of human perceptual evaluation: Given that the paper explicitly positions itself around human preference and perceptual aesthetics, relying solely on automated reward models (ImageReward, HPSv2, LAION aesthetic score) without a user study leaves aesthetic enhancement claims partially unsubstantiated.

strengths: The paper presents an interesting and novel perspective on training-free DiT acceleration: exploiting the spatial non-uniformity induced by aesthetic and stylistic descriptors in prompts to allocate inference compute and guidance preferentially to perceptually salient regions.

The evaluation is unusually extensive in scale for an inference acceleration paper, conducting experiments across 10,000 Pick-a-Pic prompts with 3 fixed seeds (30,000 images per configuration) and benchmarking against multiple competitive baselines (TeaCache, TaylorSeer, Delta-DiT, RAS, SDiT, FORA).

The paper provides detailed ablation studies and diagnostic analyses, including runtime decomposition, anchor trigger statistics across datasets, anchor vocabulary frequency, and sensitivity analyses for key hyperparameters (skip_ratio, mask_step).

On Lumina-Next-T2I, AccelAes demonstrates strong empirical trade-offs, achieving a 2.11× wall-clock speedup while maintaining or moderately improving preference and aesthetic proxies (ImageReward, HPSv2, Aesthetic score).
weaknesses: Limited architectural generality for the core spatial components: As acknowledged in Appendix A.3 and Section C.5, the full AccelAes framework (AesMask + SkipSparse + Spatial CFG + StepCache) only fully functions on Lumina-Next. On SD3-Medium, spatial CFG is disabled due to instability in MMDiT blocks, and on FLUX.1-dev, spatial SkipSparse is entirely omitted, leaving FLUX to run essentially only the temporal StepCache mechanism. This significantly weakens the claim that the aesthetics-guided spatial sparsification framework is universally applicable across modern DiT backbones.

Potential confounding from guidance scale modulation: The reported gains in ImageReward and Aesthetic score appear to be driven substantially by the spatial CFG design (Eq. 11), where aesthetic-focus tokens receive a higher CFG scale ($g_{aes} \ge g_{bg} \ge 1$). Since scaling CFG is well known to increase aesthetic/contrast scores on automated reward models, it is unclear whether the perceptual improvement stems from superior compute allocation or simply from localized over-guidance. A baseline with matched/tuned CFG configurations is missing.

Reliance on an ad-hoc predefined anchor vocabulary: AesMask depends on a hard-coded set of 34 English aesthetic anchor words. In prompts lacking these stylistic descriptors (where the trigger rate on unique Pick-a-Pic prompts is only 44.9%), the method falls back to uniform attention weighting, diminishing the core aesthetic hypothesis.

Lack of human evaluation: All aesthetic and preference gains are supported solely through automated reward models (ImageReward, HPSv2, LAION Aesthetic predictor), which can suffer from reward over-optimization or stylistic biases (such as oversaturation and high edge density). A blind user study would be necessary to substantiate the claim of genuine perceptual aesthetic enhancement.

strengths: Exploring perceptual non-uniformity across spatial tokens to allocate computational budget during Diffusion Transformer (DiT) inference is an intuitive and relevant research problem.
The evaluation uses a large-scale evaluation set of 10,000 prompts sampled from Pick-a-Pic across multiple automated preference and aesthetic metrics (ImageReward, HPSv2, LAION Aesthetic).
Combining spatial sparse attention with temporal reuse addresses two orthogonal redundancy axes in iterative diffusion sampling.
weaknesses: Severe overclaiming of architectural generalizability: Although the paper presents AccelAes as a general framework evaluated on three backbones (Lumina-Next, SD3-Medium, and FLUX.1-dev), Section A.3 reveals that the core spatial contribution (AesMask and SkipSparse) is completely disabled on FLUX.1-dev and largely bypassed on SD3-Medium. On FLUX, AccelAes reduces entirely to StepCache (temporal caching). Evaluating and claiming an aesthetics-aware spatial acceleration framework across backbones when two out of three backbones cannot execute the spatial module is misleading.

Formulation flaw in StepCache (Equations 12 and 13): Equation 12 defines $E_\tau = \hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_\tau$ and $E_{\tau+\Delta} = \hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{\tau+\Delta}$, and Equation 13 uses both to approximate $\hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_t$ for intermediate steps $t \in (\tau, \tau+\Delta)$. In standard sequential diffusion sampling, step $\tau+\Delta$ is in the future and cannot be evaluated prior to intermediate steps $t$. If this is linear extrapolation from past steps, the indices and formulation ($E_{\tau+\Delta}$ and $\lambda(t)$) are mathematically erroneous; if it is interpolation, the execution flow is physically impossible in autoregressive generation without lookahead.

Confounding acceleration with guidance modulation: The reported gains in aesthetic and preference metrics (e.g., ImageReward, LAION Aesthetic) over the dense baseline appear to stem from modifying the classifier-free guidance scale in Eq. 11 (Spatial CFG), rather than from computation reduction. Increasing CFG on salient tokens is well known to boost contrast, CLIP score, and aesthetic metrics at the expense of distribution coverage. There is no fair ablation comparing the dense baseline under the same guidance modulation.

Heuristic and narrow anchor mechanism: AesMask relies on an ad-hoc dictionary of 34 English words. As reported in Table 12, this mechanism fails to trigger on over 55% of unique prompts in Pick-a-Pic, requiring a fallback to uniform weighting. This reliance on explicit stylistic adjectives limits the robustness and utility of the method on natural or descriptive prompts.

Unresolved empirical contradictions: In the Lumina ablation (Table 7), running StepCache alone degrades ImageReward from 0.752 to 0.743. However, on SD3-Medium and FLUX.1-dev—where the spatial path is disabled and AccelAes relies exclusively on StepCache—the method is reported to significantly outperform the dense baseline on ImageReward and aesthetic score. The paper provides no plausible explanation for how uniform step skipping alone enhances generative quality on FLUX and SD3 while degrading it on Lumina.
Poor presentation and corrupted figures: Key quantitative plots (Figure 3 and Figure 4b) suffer from severe rendering errors, with corrupted fonts, missing glyphs, and unreadable axes.

strengths: The core insight—linking prompt aesthetic semantics and cross-attention non-uniformity to spatial compute budgeting and regional guidance in DiTs—is novel, intuitive, and well-motivated compared to purely uniform or heuristic token reduction methods.
The method is training-free and modular, coupling spatial sparse attention/FFN computation (SkipSparse) with temporal output-level step caching (StepCache).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple modern DiT architectures (Lumina-Next, SD3-Medium, FLUX.1-dev) against numerous recent training-free acceleration baselines (TeaCache, TaylorSeer, Δ-DiT, FORA, RAS, SDiT).

The paper is very thorough in its supplementary analysis, featuring end-to-end runtime breakdowns, blind human preference evaluation, prompt robustness tests on complex scenes, and sensitivity analyses for key hyperparameters (skip_ratio, mask_step).
weaknesses: Uneven applicability across architectures: The full spatial acceleration pipeline (AesMask + SkipSparse + Spatial CFG) only fully applies to Lumina-Next. In SD3-Medium, spatial CFG had to be disabled due to MMDiT joint-token instability, and in FLUX.1-dev, spatial SkipSparse could not be used at all (relying almost solely on StepCache temporal reuse). This limits the generality of the core spatial contribution across diverse transformer architectures.

Conflation of acceleration and guidance enhancement: The observed improvements in ImageReward and aesthetic score appear largely driven by the Spatial CFG mechanism (amplifying guidance on masked tokens via Eq. 11) rather than the compute reduction itself. A dense baseline with identical spatial CFG should be clearly highlighted in the main tables to disentangle the aesthetic boost from the acceleration effects.

Heuristic anchor dictionary dependency: The construction of AesMask relies on a fixed vocabulary of 34 hand-selected aesthetic anchor terms. While prompt-token matching provides a proxy, Table 19 indicates that less than 45% of prompts in the broader Pick-a-Pic pool have strong similarity (≥0.60) to these anchors, meaning the top-r ranking may select arbitrary/spurious tokens on prompts without aesthetic descriptors.

The temporal reuse mechanism (StepCache) relies on straightforward linear extrapolation between stride steps, which is relatively incremental given existing forecasting and caching literature (e.g., FORA, TaylorSeer).

strengths: Well-motivated approach connecting prompt-level aesthetic descriptors to inference-time spatial compute budgeting and localized guidance in Diffusion Transformers.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple backbones (Lumina-Next-T2I, SD3-Medium, FLUX.1-dev) against leading training-free acceleration methods (such as TeaCache, TaylorSeer, Delta-DiT, and RAS).

Thorough ablation studies and diagnostics, including component-wise speedup decompositions, sensitivity analyses on mask timing and skip ratios, anchor vocabulary hit statistics, and blind pairwise human preference validation.
Promising speedup results, demonstrating up to 2.11x wall-clock speedup on Lumina-Next while maintaining or improving automatic preference metrics (ImageReward, HPSv2, aesthetic score).
weaknesses: Limited architectural generality for the core spatial mechanism: As acknowledged in Appendix A.3, the spatial SkipSparse and spatial-CFG components cannot be uniformly applied across architectures. On SD3-Medium, spatial CFG had to be disabled due to instability in MMDiT joint attention, and on FLUX.1-dev, spatial SkipSparse was omitted entirely (relying solely on temporal StepCache). This significantly diminishes the generality of the aesthetic-guided spatial reduction claims.

Attribution of quality gains: The observed improvements in ImageReward and aesthetic score appear largely driven by the spatial CFG amplification ($g_{aes} > g_{bg}$) rather than the compute reduction itself. Comparing against baselines with equivalent localized guidance modulation would better isolate the impact of the acceleration framework.

Heuristic anchor dictionary dependency: AesMask relies on an empirical dictionary of 34 predefined text anchors matched via CLIP cosine similarity. When prompts lack explicit stylistic or aesthetic adjectives, the selection can become brittle or fall back to generic nouns/objects, creating potential inconsistency in mask quality across varied user prompt distributions.

Risk of gaming automated preference benchmarks: Metric boosts in ImageReward and edge density via increased localized guidance often correlate with higher local contrast and over-sharpening, which automated preference models favor, while human preference gains (e.g., 59% win rate on alignment in Table 3) are more modest.

strengths: Thorough empirical evaluation: Experiments are conducted over a substantial scale (10,000 prompts from Pick-a-Pic with multiple seeds, totaling 30,000 images per configuration) across multiple standard evaluation metrics (CLIP, ImageReward, HPSv2, LAION Aesthetic, Edge Density).

Comprehensive validation suite: The manuscript includes systematic ablation studies (dissecting StepCache, attention sparsification, FFN sparsification, anchor selection strategies, and skip ratios) alongside a blind pairwise human preference study.

Intuitive motivation: Linking cross-attention responsiveness with human aesthetic focus to guide token sparsification offers an interesting alternative to purely numerical or structural token pruning.
weaknesses: Severe architectural limitations and inconsistent applicability across DiT backbones: A central premise of the paper is the unified aesthetics-aware spatial sparsification framework. However, as revealed in Appendix A.3, the spatial SkipSparse module cannot be applied to FLUX.1-dev due to its unified transformer blocks, reducing AccelAes on FLUX to simple temporal prediction caching (StepCache). Furthermore, on SD3-Medium, the spatial CFG component had to be disabled due to instability in MMDiT blocks. Consequently, the core spatial contribution is only fully operational on Lumina-Next, substantially undermining the claims of generality across modern DiT architectures.

Aesthetic enhancement is largely attributable to local CFG scaling rather than acceleration: The reported aesthetic and preference gains appear to be primarily driven by the heuristic spatial CFG boost ($g_{aes} > g_{bg}$) rather than the sparsification mechanism itself. Increasing CFG on salient foreground regions is a known trick to elevate sharpness and contrast (which reward models like ImageReward favor), meaning the aesthetic gains are orthogonal to the inference acceleration.

Heuristic nature of AesMask and anchor formulation: The aesthetic focus relies on a fixed, handcrafted dictionary of 34 anchor words matched via CLIP cosine similarity. When prompts lack aesthetic qualifiers, the top-$r$ selection defaults to arbitrary content tokens. The biological/perceptual grounding of this anchor set is weakly justified.

StepCache novelty is limited: The temporal caching component (Eq. 12-13) relies on standard linear extrapolation across a fixed stride $\Delta=2$, which closely mirrors existing diffusion trajectory reuse methods (e.g., TaylorSeer, FORA) without offering significant theoretical advancement.

Formatting and review-cycle artifacts: Section E in the appendix explicitly labels sections as 'Rebuttal-Driven Additional Experiments' responding to 'reviewer concerns', indicating unedited carryover text from a previous conference review cycle.
